Selling is probably the least “perfect” part of my system, and I don’t think there’s 1 correct way to do it.

What’s helped me is realizing I can keep the same management framework while adjusting how much leash I give positions depending on the environment.

In a healthy trending market, I WANT to sit. I’ll trim in fourths/fifths into expansion & ATR extensions from the MAs, get my risk to breakeven once I’ve paid myself, then give the remaining position room against the 9/21EMA or important pivots. If a leader is acting correctly, I’m trying my hardest not to interrupt something that could turn into a 3-5 day momentum move or eventually a position trade.

Chop is different. If the market keeps showing me that breakouts are failing, stocks are going +5% and giving back +4%, and follow-through isn’t being rewarded, I adapt.

I’ll buy closer to support instead of through obvious breakouts, take the first trim quicker into strength, move my stop to breakeven, and become much less emotionally attached to holding for the home run. I’m basically trying to get cushion as quickly as possible because I know the environment has been taking it away.

Also, 1 thing I’m VERY conscious of, though, is not letting “it’s choppy” become an excuse to butcher every winner. If a stock is showing abnormal RS, its group is working, volume is strong, and it keeps closing near highs, I’ll give THAT position more leash regardless of what the indices are doing. I want price to earn my patience!!

So I personally don’t try to solve selling with some magical “always sell at +10%” rule. I simply ask: Is this environment rewarding holding? Is this stock rewarding holding? Have I built enough cushion to sit through normal volatility? Then I manage from there.

That’s just what has worked for me.

I’m still constantly refining it, but my basic rule is when the market is paying me to sit, I sit, and when it keeps taking back my cushion, I pay myself faster.

I don't want to sell the top, because that's unrealistic. I want to keep enough of the move when I’m right without letting every good trade turn back into nothing.

One of the biggest mistakes new traders make is searching for indicators instead of searching for a structural edge.
Structural edge is a market behaviour that has existed for decades.

In one of his 2014 blog posts, Pradeep highlighted examples such as:
- Markets move in momentum bursts
- Momentum stocks outperform non-momentum stocks
- Surprisingly good earnings often lead to sustained rallies
- News drives immediate price moves
- Small-cap / low-float stocks often outperform
Once you've identified one, finding the edge is only Step 1.

The real work is building a repeatable trading template around it:
• Which stocks qualify?
• Entry? Stop? Position size? Exit?
• When do you stay out?
That's what separates a good idea from a profitable trading system.
